strongest_bounded_proposition: Slavery was structurally embedded in the Mamluk Sultanate around 1300: military slaves formed the ruling military-political elite while domestic and labour slavery also existed in Egypt and Syria.
strongest_unsupported_proposition: Do not equate elite mamluk military status with every enslaved person's experience or infer one prevalence rate across Egypt and Syria.
territorial_practice_summary: Military, domestic and labour slavery are directly supported.
legal_state_summary: Islamic legal/manumission frameworks structured slavery but did not make all statuses equivalent.
external_network_summary: The sultanate depended on imported enslaved people for military and domestic markets.
terminology_category_qualification: Mamluk can describe a particular military-slave trajectory; most enslaved people were not elite mamluks.
temporal_scope_precision: Sources directly cover the Mamluk Sultanate 1250–1517 and therefore the 1300 anchor.
inference_extent: Institutional occurrence and multiple forms; no one prevalence score.
language_access_limitations: English-accessible research packet only; non-English and non-digitized scholarship was not exhaustively searched.
